H1.text: A roller coaster loops the loop. A toy car loops its track. A bucket of water swings over your head.

H2.text: All three go upside down at the top. So why does nothing fall?

H3.text: Aarav swings a bucket of water over his head, in the college corridor.

H4.text: Fast, and not a drop falls. Slow, and he gets wet. How slow is too slow?

H5.text: By the end, you will find that speed with one short formula.

P1.text: So what is motion in a vertical circle?

P2.text: It is going round a circle that stands up, like a wheel on the road.

P3.text: Going up, gravity slows the ball. Coming down, it speeds it up. So the speed keeps changing.

P4.text: Two forces act. The string's pull, called tension, T. And the weight, m g.

P5.text: Their total pull toward the centre must be m v squared over r. That bends the path into a circle.

S1.text: A half kilogram ball on a one metre string, seen from the side.

S2.text: Start it at five metres per second at the bottom. It slows as it climbs.

S3.text: Just past the side, the tension hits zero. The string goes slack, and the ball falls inside.

S4.text: Now start it at seven metres per second. It just makes it over the top.

S5.text: On the graph, the pull is biggest at the bottom, twenty nine point four newtons, and zero at the top.

S6.text: Slow-mo replay, at the very top.

S7.text: The string is not pulling. Gravity alone pulls the ball to the centre, and it is just enough.

D1.text: Now let's find that speed, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. At the top, T and m g both point down, toward the centre. So T plus m g equals m v squared over r.

D3.text: Step two. A string can pull, but never push. So the slowest case is T equals zero.

D4.text: Step three. Then m g equals m v squared over r. Cancel m. The top speed is root g r.

D5.text: Step four. Energy. From the top, the ball drops two r. So v bottom squared is v top squared plus four g r. Root five g r.

T1.text: Remember this. On a string, the top speed must be at least root g r.

C1.text: Now, the bottom and the top, side by side.

C2.text: At the bottom, the weight pulls away from the centre. So the string holds the weight, and gives m v squared over r too. T is biggest.

C3.text: At the top, the weight already pulls toward the centre. The string does less. T is smallest.

C4.text: Now you try. A weak rope. Where will it snap first, at the bottom or at the top? Pause and decide.

C5.text: At the bottom! There the rope holds the weight, and also bends the path.

K2.text: Now swap the string for a stiff rod, which can also push. On a rod, what is the slowest top speed? Root g r, or almost zero? Pause and decide.

K3.text: Almost zero! If the ball is slow, the rod pushes it up. It only has to reach the top.

R1.text: So why does Aarav's water stay in? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. At the top, the water needs a pull of m v squared over r, downward.

R3.text: Two. Its weight, m g, gives some. The bucket base pushes down to give the rest.

R4.text: Three. Swung fast, m v squared over r is more than m g. The base presses, and the water stays.

R5.text: Four. Swung slowly, m g is more than needed. Gravity pulls the water out of the circle. He gets wet.

W2.text: Aarav's bucket holds one kilogram of water, on a circle of radius zero point nine metres.

W3.text: The slowest top speed is root g r. Root of nine point eight times zero point nine. About three metres per second.

W4.text: At the bottom, v squared is five g r. That is forty four point one.

W5.text: So the base pushes up with m g plus m v squared over r. Nine point eight plus forty nine. Fifty eight point eight newtons.

W6.text: Six times the water's weight. His arm feels it at the bottom.

X2.text: Many students write the top equation as T equals m v squared over r, plus m g.

X3.text: But at the top, gravity points toward the centre too. So T equals m v squared over r, minus m g.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In numericals on top and bottom speeds, and the tension at a point.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A point two kilogram ball whirls in a vertical circle on a one metre string. The top tension is three newtons, and g is ten. Find the bottom tension. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Fifteen newtons.

A2.text: At the top, T plus m g is m v squared over r. Three plus two is five, so v top squared is twenty five.

A3.text: Energy. Down two metres, v bottom squared is twenty five plus forty, sixty five.

A4.text: At the bottom, T is m g plus m v squared over r. Two plus thirteen. Fifteen newtons.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does the speed change on a vertical circle?

Y3.text: Two. Why can the top speed on a string not be zero?

Y4.text: Three. Where does the string pull hardest, and why?

N1.text: Next time: two friends climb the same stairs, one faster. Who has more power? We find out in power.
